source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

Her boarding pass was in order, and she was waved through. The officer was thorough, checking the traveler's documents against the manifest, then nodding to an aide, who stood by with a handheld scanner. She was cleared, and the line crept onward, slowed by the security checks. A sign above the checkpoint read "Remove electronics and liquids" in bold red letters, a message reinforced by a video screen. The officer's expression was courteous but firm as she questioned the traveler, her eyes flicking between the face and the passport photo. The traveler complied, producing a boarding pass and a valid visa, and was released into the concourse. As they passed through, a voice murmured, and a second officer nodded, making a note on a handheld device. Meanwhile, the line continued to shuffle forward, its progress monitored by the CCTV cameras. The young woman, now cleared, walked briskly away, merging into the flow of passengers. And though the security check was thorough, it was performed with a practiced courtesy that belied its rigor.
